check:0:0.q: Why not “No: the policy sees every change to the account”?
check:0:0.a:
That answer gets one thing right. Inside Spacelift, the policy really does check every run. Every plan for the Foundation or Service stack passes through it. Even a replacement, which is a delete followed by a create, gets caught.

What it misses is the word "account." The policy never watches the storage account itself. It only reads the **plan**, the list of changes Terraform proposes for one Spacelift run. If a change never becomes a Spacelift plan, the policy never sees it.

So a storage account can still disappear in other ways:

- Someone with enough Azure rights deletes it in the Azure portal, the web console for Azure.
- Someone runs a delete command with the Azure CLI, the command-line tool for Azure.
- Someone runs `terraform destroy` on their own laptop, skipping Spacelift entirely.
- Someone deletes the whole resource group, the Azure folder that holds the account.

None of these meet the policy. That's why teams also add Azure resource locks and keep powerful rights tightly limited.

"Yes: a delete outside Spacelift never meets the policy" is better because it names the real limit: the policy guards the Spacelift pipeline, not the resource.

judge.notes: No major problems; the Azure resource locks and the portal, CLI and laptop examples go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Only if the Rego rule has a bug”?
check:0:2.a:
"Only if the Rego rule has a bug" gets one thing right. A buggy rule can miss a delete. For example, if the protected set spells the type wrong, or the rule ignores replacements, a storage account could slip through.

But it assumes the policy sees every change. It doesn't. A plan policy only runs inside Spacelift. It reads the plan (Terraform's list of proposed changes) for that run, and nothing else.

So a perfect rule still can't stop deletes that never become a Spacelift plan:

- Someone removes the storage account in the Azure portal.
- Someone runs `az storage account delete` from the Azure CLI (the command-line tool for Azure).
- Someone runs `terraform destroy` on their own laptop against the PROD state.

None of these create a Spacelift run, so the policy never gets a chance to check them. The policy is a guardrail on one road, not a wall around the resource.

"Yes: a delete outside Spacelift never meets the policy" is better because it names the real limit: the policy only checks what goes through Spacelift.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Only if the reviewer turns it on”?
check:1:1.a:
"Only if the reviewer turns it on" gets one thing right. People still matter in this process. In Spacelift, a run goes from a proposed plan, to policy checks, to an apply that someone approves. A human reviewer is still part of that.

What it misses is the main point of a plan policy. A plan policy runs automatically on every Spacelift run. Nobody switches it on for each run. It checks the plan by itself, whether the reviewer is alert or half asleep.

That matters on a Friday evening. Picture a tired reviewer skimming a plan for team-sales in PROD. Say that plan would destroy a Databricks workspace or a storage account. The reviewer might miss it. The policy still reads every change and can block the run. If the policy depended on the reviewer, it would fail exactly when you need it most. That's why the lesson calls it "code review that never gets tired."

"Yes, it runs on every run by itself" is better because it states the key fact: the guardrail works on every run without depending on anyone's attention.

check:1:2.q: Why not “No, it waits for a person to look”?
check:1:2.a:
That answer gets one thing right. A person does still take part. In Spacelift, a stack goes from a proposed plan to policy checks to an approved apply, and a human gives that approval.

But it mixes up two separate steps. The plan policy doesn't wait for anyone. It runs automatically on every run, right after the plan is made. So it checks the plan whether the reviewer reads closely, skims, or is already halfway out the door on Friday.

That's the whole point of a policy. It's code review that never gets tired. Picture a Friday change to team-sales in PROD whose plan would destroy a workspace. The tired reviewer might miss that line. The policy won't. It sees a delete on a protected resource type and blocks the run before anyone can approve it.

The human review and the policy work together. The policy just doesn't depend on the human.

"Yes, it runs on every run by itself" is better because it captures what a plan policy is: an automatic check that doesn't rely on a reviewer paying attention.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The only soft spot is that 'a human gives that approval' goes slightly beyond the lesson's 'approved apply', but it is a reasonable reading.

check:2:0.a:
"Tags on every resource" isn't a bad policy. Tags are labels on Azure resources, like `owner = grp-sales-dev-owners` or a cost center. A rule that requires them keeps billing and ownership clear. Many platform teams add one eventually.

But it's not the first thing to protect. The lesson's advice is to start with what you can't rebuild. A missing tag is cheap to fix. You add it to the YAML, run the stack again, and nothing is lost.

A deleted workspace or storage account is different. Notebooks, jobs, permissions and data for `team-sales` can be gone. Re-running Terraform recreates an empty shell, not what was inside.

A tag rule is also noisy at the start. It checks every resource, so it may block lots of runs. Teams can start ignoring a policy that keeps blocking them over small things. That weakens the guardrail. A guardrail is a safety check that stops the worst mistakes.

"Storage accounts and workspaces" is better because blocking their accidental destruction protects the things whose loss is permanent, which is where an automatic check pays off most.

judge.notes: No real problems; the claims that tag rules are noisy and that many teams add them eventually go beyond the lesson, but they don't contradict it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Clusters people start by hand”?
check:2:2.a:
It gets one thing right. Clusters matter, and teams like team-sales use them every day. But it misses two things.

First, a plan policy only sees what's in the Terraform plan. The plan is Terraform's list of proposed changes for a run. A cluster someone starts by hand in the Databricks UI isn't managed by Terraform. So it never shows up in `input.terraform.resource_changes`, and the policy has nothing to check.

Second, clusters are easy to replace. If one goes away, someone can start a new one in a few minutes.

The lesson says to start with the resources you can't rebuild: workspaces, storage accounts and metastores. A metastore is the top-level catalog that tracks a region's data and permissions. Deleting one of these by accident is the costly mistake that a reviewer who never gets tired should catch first.

"Storage accounts and workspaces" is better because they appear in the plan, and they're the resources you can't rebuild if a run deletes them.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Protect the resources you can't rebuild” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Terraform can rebuild the *shell* of a resource, but not what lives inside it. A workspace holds notebooks, job history and people's work. The lake storage account holds the actual data files. The metastore (the central list of catalogs, tables and who may read them) holds every table registration and grant. None of that lives in your Terraform code. Destroy the resource and it is gone, even if `apply` creates a fresh, empty one a minute later.

Here is how it slips through. Someone fixes a typo in the storage account's name in the Foundation stage code. Azure can't rename a storage account. So the plan (Terraform's preview of its changes) shows a replacement: delete the old one, then create a new one. In a long plan, that line is easy to miss. A tired reviewer approves it in PROD. The new account is empty, and team-sales's tables now point at nothing.

A plan policy that makes these deletes an error stops the run before apply. Tiredness can't wave it through.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The policy never says anything.** Weeks of runs and zero denials can look like good news. Often it means the rule never matches at all.
- **A replacement slips through.** Terraform sometimes swaps a resource out instead of editing it. For example, changing the region of the `team-sales` workspace forces this. The plan shows "destroy and recreate", yet the run still goes ahead. That usually means the rule was written to catch a plain delete only.
- **A typo in a protected type.** If `azurerm_databricks_workspace` is misspelled in your set, nothing errors. It just silently protects nothing.
- **The policy isn't attached to every stack.** It guards the DEV Foundation stack but not the PROD Service stack. A "stack" is one Spacelift setup that runs one stage in one environment.

**Quickest check**

In DEV, make a change you know forces a workspace or storage account to be replaced. Open a proposed run, which is the plan-only preview. It should be blocked with a clear message naming the resource address. Then look at the policy results in the run's details on each stack. Confirm the policy actually ran there.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Renaming a resource in code.** If someone renames the workspace module for `team-sales`, Terraform sees a new name and plans a delete plus a create. The policy blocks it, which is correct, because the real workspace would be destroyed. Add a `moved` block, a note telling Terraform "this is the same thing under a new name," so the plan shows no delete.

**2. Precious things not on your list.** The set only protects the types you put in it, so a Unity Catalog catalog or a storage container holding `team-sales` data slips through if it's missing. Review the set whenever a module starts creating a new resource type.

**3. A teardown you actually want.** Sometimes you really do mean to retire a workspace, such as an old DEV one. Don't delete or weaken the policy for this. Give it a deliberate escape hatch instead, such as a label on the stack or an extra approver, so the destroy happens on purpose and leaves a record.

learn:term.a:
Think of a building inspector who reviews every blueprint before work starts. The inspector builds nothing. They just read the plan and say "fine," "be careful," or "stop."

A **plan policy** is that inspector for Spacelift. Each stack, like the Service stage for a workspace, first makes a plan. A plan is Terraform's list of what it intends to create, change or delete. Before anyone approves the apply, the plan policy reads that list automatically, on every run. It can warn, or it can block.

In the lesson's Rego example, `input.terraform.resource_changes` is that list of planned changes. The rule looks at each change, called `rc`, and checks two things:

- Does `rc.change.actions` contain `"delete"`?
- Is `rc.type` in `protected`, the set of types you can't rebuild, like workspaces, storage accounts and metastores?

When both are true, the rule adds a message to `deny`, such as "`azurerm_databricks_workspace.sales_dev` would be destroyed." That message blocks the run.

A replacement's actions include delete, so the rule catches replacements too.

check:0:0.q: Why not “So the run still applies while the rule is test…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option isn't wrong about the facts. A **warn** rule does let the run carry on. Spacelift prints the message in yellow, and the plan can still be approved and applied.

But it describes a side effect, not the reason. Letting runs through is just how a warning behaves. The point of starting with one is what you **learn** during that time.

Say you add the rule "no public network access." While it only warns, you watch the yellow messages on real runs. Maybe it flags the workspace for `team-sales` in DEV, as expected. Maybe it also flags something you didn't mean to catch, because the rule was written too broadly. That kind of wrong flag is called a **false positive**. You fix the rule, and nobody's run got blocked by your mistake. Then you switch it to **deny**, which blocks the run in red.

"So the run still applies" doesn't say what you gain from those runs.

"To see what it would block before it blocks anyone" is better because it names the real goal: checking the rule's results against real changes before it can stop any team's work.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Because a deny rule needs an admin to approve it”?
check:0:2.a:
That option mixes up two different things.

**What it gets close to:** a deny rule is strict. When it fires, the Spacelift run stops in red. Someone then has to fix the change, or adjust the rule, before the stack can move on.

**What it misses:** nothing in a plan policy says a deny rule needs an admin to approve it. "Deny" just means "block this run." Approval is a separate step in the stack: a person approves the apply after the plan and the policy checks. So the option gives a reason that isn't true, and it skips the real worry.

The real worry is surprise. A brand-new rule, like "no public network access," might match changes you didn't expect. For example, it might catch an existing workspace for `team-sales` in DEV that was set up before the rule existed. As a deny rule on day one, it could block that team's runs with no warning.

**Why "To see what it would block before it blocks anyone" is better:** a warning prints in yellow and lets the run through, so you learn what the rule catches and can fix it before it ever stops real work.

judge.notes: No real problems; it is close to the 200-word limit, and calling deny's strictness 'what it gets close to' is a slight stretch since the option's claim is false.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Never destroy data you can't recreate”?
check:1:1.a:
"Never destroy data you can't recreate" is a real rule from this lesson, and it matters. It just isn't the one this plan breaks.

That rule asks two things about a change: is this a protected type, and is the action a delete? It only fires when both are true. Here, nothing is being deleted. So whichever types your team marks as protected, rule 1 has nothing to say. The storage account and its data stay where they are.

The risk in this plan is different. Turning on public access means anyone on the internet can try to reach that storage account. Nothing is lost, but it is exposed. Rule 1 never looks at access settings, so it would let this change through.

That is why each rule checks every change on its own. Each one asks a separate question. A change can pass one rule and still break another.

"Never open things to the public internet" is the better answer because it checks the exact setting this plan changes: whether public access is switched on.

check:1:2.a:
"Always tag every resource" is a real rule many platform teams use. Tags are labels on a resource, like `owner = grp-sales-dev-owners` or `env = dev`. They help you track who owns something and what it costs. So the instinct to want rules like this is sound.

But it doesn't fit this plan. A tagging rule only asks, "Does this resource have its labels?" It never looks at network settings. Picture a storage account for `team-sales` with perfect tags and public access turned on. The tagging rule would pass it, and the data would still be open to anyone on the internet.

Also, tagging isn't one of the two rules this lesson builds. The lesson's rules are "never destroy data you can't recreate" and "never open things to the public internet." Nothing is being deleted here, so rule 1 stays quiet. The plan's only problem is the network opening.

"Never open things to the public internet" is the better answer because it checks the exact setting this plan is changing, public network access, and blocks or warns on it.

judge.notes: No real problems. The remark that tagging is a common real-world rule goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Make the wiki page easier to find”?
check:2:0.a:
Making the wiki page easier to find does fix one real problem. Someone new might not know the rule exists, and a clear link helps them learn it.

But that probably isn't what went wrong last Friday. The rule was written down. The delete still slipped through. That means a reviewer, maybe rushing through a PROD Service stack plan, didn't stop to check. A page that's easier to find is still a page someone has to remember to open, read and apply by hand. On a busy day, that step is exactly the one that gets skipped.

So the rule still lives in people's heads, with a link attached. Nothing actually checks the plan. A delete of team-sales' catalog or workspace can still reach an approved apply.

A plan policy is a rule written as code that Spacelift runs on every proposed plan. It looks at every change on its own. If it spots a protected resource being deleted, it can **deny** the run, meaning it blocks the run and shows the reason in red.

"Turn it into a plan policy" is better because the check then runs automatically on every plan and can block the run, so it no longer depends on anyone remembering it.

judge.notes: No real problems; it is about 205 words, slightly over the 200 guide, and it guesses at why Friday's delete slipped through, though it hedges with 'probably' and 'maybe'.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Add a line to the review checklist”?
check:2:1.a:
A checklist line gets one thing right. It writes the rule down where reviewers will see it. That's better than a wiki page nobody opens.

But it misses the real problem. The checklist still depends on a person reading it and doing it. The delete slipped through last Friday because someone was busy and skipped a step. A checklist is just the same wiki rule in a new spot. On the next busy day, someone can tick the box without really looking.

Picture a Service stack plan for `team-sales` in PROD that deletes a catalog. A tired reviewer scrolls past it, ticks "checked for deletes," and approves. Nothing stops them.

A **plan policy** is a rule written as code that Spacelift runs on every proposed plan, before anyone approves it. It doesn't get tired or skip steps. If you set it to **deny**, which means block the run, that PROD delete stops in red no matter how rushed the team is.

"Turn it into a plan policy" is better because the check runs by itself on every plan, so it can't be skipped.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Every run is green, forever.** No warnings, no denials, ever. That's too clean. Product teams will sometimes ask for risky things. A silent policy is often one that isn't checking.
- **Only one message when there should be two.** Say a change to `team-sales` both deletes a protected catalog and turns public access on. If the log shows just the "would be destroyed" message, the rules are blocking each other. Each rule should check every change on its own.
- **A surprise in Azure.** Someone finds a PROD workspace with `public_network_access_enabled` set to true, but every Spacelift run passed. The rule missed it, or it never ran on that stack. A stack is one stage that Spacelift runs.
- **Yellow that never turns red.** A rule stays a warning for months. People learn to scroll past it, so it blocks nothing.

**Quickest check**

On a DEV stack, push a deliberately bad change. Delete a protected resource and open it to the public internet in the same change. You should see both messages in the plan output, rule 1 first. The plan is Terraform's preview of what it would change. If one message is missing, or the run goes green, the policy isn't doing its job.

judge.notes: No major problem; it is about 205 words, right at the length limit, and the 'yellow never turns red' sign goes slightly beyond the lesson but fits its warn-first advice.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where this approach needs extra care.

**A new kind of resource shows up.** Rule 1 only knows the protected types you listed. A protected type is a kind of resource that holds data you can't recreate. If the platform starts using a new resource like that, deleting it slips through, so add it to the list and roll that change out as a warning first.

**A team has a real reason for an exception.** Say team-sales needs a short-lived public test setup in DEV only. Don't switch the rule off for everyone. Write one narrow, named exception for that case, and keep the deny in UAT and PROD.

**The rule list grows long.** With many rules, one change can print several messages, and people start ignoring yellow warnings. Once a warning has proven it only flags real problems, promote it to a deny. Keep each message specific about the resource and the fix.

learn:term.a:
Both are outcomes a Spacelift plan policy can give when a rule matches a change. A plan is Terraform's preview of what it will create, change or delete.

**Deny** blocks the run. The stack shows red, and nothing gets applied until someone fixes the plan.

**Warn** prints the message in yellow but lets the run carry on. People see it, but nobody is stopped.

Think of a new speed camera. For the first month it only sends "you were speeding" letters. Once drivers know it's there, it starts handing out fines.

That's how the two work together. Say you add rule 2: never open workspaces or storage to the public internet. You start it as a warning. Suppose a plan for `team-sales` turns on `public_network_access_enabled` for its DEV workspace. The run still goes through, but "... allows public network access" shows in yellow.

After a few runs, you know which stacks would trip the rule. You also learn whether it's too strict. Fix those stacks, then switch the rule to deny so it blocks for real.

check:0:1.q: Why not “A test with two catalogs in it”?
check:0:1.a:
A test with two catalogs isn't wrong. It could catch something real. If a plan deletes `databricks_catalog.sales` and `databricks_catalog.finance`, you'd expect `count(deny) == 2`, one message per catalog. That checks the rule loops through every change, not just the first.

But it tests the same direction as the test you already have. Both hand the policy a bad plan and check that it says no. A rule that denies *everything* would pass both. Picture a rule that blocks every plan, even team-sales adding `databricks_schema.raw` in DEV. Your tests stay green. You find out on Monday when every team's runs are stuck.

That's the door lock again. Trying a second wrong key tells you nothing new. A lock that never opens also keeps burglars out.

"A test that a safe plan is allowed" is better because it checks the other direction. It proves the rule lets good plans through, which is the one thing your current test can't show.

judge.notes: No major problems; the only slight tension is that it says a two-catalog test 'could catch something real' and later that a second wrong key 'tells you nothing new'.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing: one test is enough”?
check:0:2.a:
"Nothing: one test is enough" gets one thing right. The test you have is useful. It proves the rule stops a plan that deletes a catalog like `databricks_catalog.sales`. That is the job the policy exists to do.

What it misses is the other half. A passing test only tells you the rule said "deny" when it should. It says nothing about whether the rule also says "deny" when it shouldn't. Picture a broken rule that denies every plan, no matter what changes. It would pass your one test too.

Think of a door lock. Trying a wrong key and seeing the door stay shut proves little. A lock that never opens also keeps burglars out. You only trust it after the right key opens it.

With one test, a too-strict rule could slip into Spacelift unnoticed. Then on Monday morning `team-sales` tries to add a schema, and every run is blocked.

"A test that a safe plan is allowed" is better because it checks that the rule lets good plans through, so the two tests together show the rule tells safe changes from dangerous ones.

check:1:0.q: Why not “A plan creating a schema”?
check:1:0.a:
A plan creating a schema isn't a bad test. It's the "let through" half of the pair. It checks that the rule doesn't block ordinary work, like team-sales adding `databricks_schema.raw` in DEV. The lesson's own example uses it for exactly that.

But the question asks something narrower. Does the rule also catch a **replacement**? A replacement is when Terraform can't change a resource in place, so it deletes it and creates a new one. In a plan this shows as `-/+`.

A schema-create plan never touches a catalog, and it never deletes anything. So the rule's answer tells you nothing about replacements. It would pass whether the rule handles them or not.

A replacement looks like this in the plan:

```
"type": "databricks_catalog",
"change": {"actions": ["delete", "create"]}
```

The rule checks whether `"delete"` is in `actions`. A test with this plan shows whether that check fires when `"delete"` comes paired with `"create"`.

A `-/+` catalog plan is better because it gives the rule exactly the tricky case, a catalog whose actions include a delete hidden inside a replacement, and shows whether the rule stops it.

check:1:2.a:
An empty plan is a plan with no changes in it. `input.terraform.resource_changes` is an empty list, so the rule has nothing to look at and denies nothing.

What it gets right: it is a fair "let through" check. A plan that changes nothing should never be blocked. If your policy denied an empty plan, you would want to know.

What it misses: the question is about replacements. A replacement is when Terraform must destroy a catalog and build a new one, shown as `-/+` in the plan, with actions `["delete", "create"]`. An empty plan holds no catalog at all, so it holds no replacement. The test passes the same way whether the rule catches replacements or not. It cannot tell a rule that works from one that is broken, so it teaches you nothing about this case.

A plan with a `-/+` catalog is better because it puts `["delete", "create"]` in front of the rule, so the test passes only if the rule really treats a replacement as a delete.

check:2:1.a:
"Whether OPA needs updating" isn't a silly thought. OPA (Open Policy Agent) is the tool that runs your Rego tests, and when something breaks it's natural to suspect the tool first.

But look at what a FAIL actually says. OPA ran the test. It handed the rule the made-up plan from `with input as {...}`. It got an answer. That answer didn't match what the test expected. So the tool did its job. It found a disagreement between your rule and your test.

That disagreement points to one of two places:

- **The rule is wrong.** Say a `-/+` replacement on `databricks_catalog.sales` slips through, but it should be denied.
- **The test is wrong.** Say the made-up plan has a typo, like `"databricks_catalogs"`, so it never looks like a real catalog change.

Updating OPA fixes neither one. You'd lose time, and the real bug would still be waiting.

"Whether the rule or the test is wrong" is better because a failing test means those two disagree, so the fix lives in one of them.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Whether to delete the test”?
check:2:2.a:
A failing test means the rule and the test disagree. One of them is wrong. "Whether to delete the test" jumps straight to a fix before you know which one.

It does get one thing right. Sometimes the test really is the problem. Maybe its made-up plan doesn't look like a real one, or it expects the old behavior. Then changing or removing it is fair.

But deleting first skips the question that matters. Say `test_replacing_a_catalog_is_denied` fails. Its plan has `["delete", "create"]` for `databricks_catalog.sales`. If you delete that test, the failure goes away. If the bug was in the rule, a replacement could now slip through to PROD and wipe the catalog. The test was the only thing warning you.

A failing test is a signal, like a smoke alarm. Pulling the battery stops the noise, not the fire.

"Whether the rule or the test is wrong" is better because it makes you find out which side is broken before you change anything, so you fix the real problem.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **All green, but teams are stuck.** `opa test policies/` prints PASS for everything. Then team-sales's DEV run is blocked for adding a schema. The tests only checked plans the rule must stop, so nobody saw it blocking good ones.
- **All green, but a catalog vanishes.** A replacement of `databricks_catalog.sales` reaches PROD. No test used a `["delete", "create"]` plan, so nobody checked how the rule treats a replacement.
- **Lopsided test file.** Every test expects `count(deny) == 1`. No test expects zero.
- **Fake plans that don't look real.** A misspelled key like `resource_change` means the rule never matches. An "allowed" test then passes, but only by luck.

**Quickest check**

First, pair them up. Each rule should have at least one plan to stop and one to let through.

Then break the rule on purpose. For example, change `"databricks_catalog"` to a wrong type, and run `opa test policies/` again. If nothing fails, your tests aren't really checking that rule.

Last, compare your made-up plans with a real sample from Spacelift's policy workbench. The workbench keeps samples only if the policy has a `sample` rule.

learn:stops.a:
**When the real plans change shape.** Your tests use made-up plans, and those only help while they match real ones. A `databricks` provider upgrade (the plugin Terraform uses to talk to Databricks) can change how a plan looks, so tests still PASS while real deletes slip by. After each upgrade, copy fresh real inputs from the policy workbench and update your test plans.

**When the rule reads more than the plan.** Some rules also look at stack details, like a label saying a stack is PROD. Then one stop-plan and one allow-plan is not enough, because the same catalog delete might be fine in DEV but blocked in PROD. Write both-way tests for each stage the rule treats differently.

**When many policies run together.** Each rule can pass its own tests, yet two rules together might still block every team's Service stack runs. As the admin repo grows, add a few tests built from a normal real run, such as team-sales adding a schema. Check that the whole set of policies lets that run through.

judge.notes: Nothing contradicts the lesson. The provider-upgrade and stack-label points go beyond it but are plausible. It also leaves out that the workbench only keeps samples if the policy has a `sample` rule.

learn:term.a:
`test_` is a name tag. It tells the test runner, "this rule is a test, run me."

Think of a logbook for a cluster review. An inspector only reads the lines that start with "CHECK:". Every other line is notes. The label is how they know what to inspect.

`opa test policies/` works the same way. OPA is the tool that runs Rego. It looks through every `.rego` file in the `policies/` folder. It picks out each rule whose name starts with `test_`, runs it, and prints PASS or FAIL. A test passes when everything inside its braces comes out true.

In the lesson's example there are two:

- `test_deleting_a_catalog_is_denied` hands `deny` a fake plan that deletes `databricks_catalog.sales`. It expects one message.
- `test_adding_a_schema_is_allowed` hands it a plan that creates `databricks_schema.raw`. It expects zero messages.

`deny` has no `test_` at the start. So OPA treats it as the policy itself, not a test.

The rest of the name is up to you. Make it say what should happen. Then when a test fails, its name tells you which promise broke.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only slip is that it states the definition before the everyday comparison, though the brief asked for the comparison first.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Everything in the plan: it finished and passed …”?
check:0:0.a:
That option reads the right clues but draws the wrong conclusion.

**What it gets right:** the run really did finish, and the GO lines really are passed checks. `FINISHED` and "Plan checks are GO" are both true facts from the screen.

**What it misses:** the run type. A **proposed** run is a preview. Spacelift starts one for a push to a branch that isn't the stack's tracked branch, such as a pull request adding `grp-sales-uat-owners` to a folder. It plans, reports back to the pull request, and stops. It never reaches the apply step, which is the step that actually changes the UAT workspace.

So `FINISHED` here only means "planning worked." The GO lines only mean automatic steps passed, like the plan running and its JSON being made. None of them is a deployment, and none is a person approving.

Think of the parcel tracking page: "label printed" is a finished step, but the parcel hasn't arrived.

"Nothing: a proposed run only previews" is better because it reads type and state together, and a proposed run can never deploy, however well it finished.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Only the resources the policies approved”?
check:0:2.a:
This option is tempting because the log talks about checks, and policies are part of the Spacelift flow. But it mixes up checking with deploying.

Start with the run type. **Proposed** means a preview. Spacelift plans, reports back to the pull request, and stops. It never applies, which means it never actually makes the changes. So nothing reached the UAT workspace. **FINISHED** on a proposed run only means planning worked.

The GO wording doesn't change that. Every GO marks one automatic step that passed, like the plan running or its JSON being made. Only the GO right after **Evaluated N plan policies** is the policies' result. Even that one is a check on a plan, not a deploy. And no GO is a person approving.

So "Only the resources the policies approved" assumes some resources were deployed. On a proposed run, none were. Deploying needs a tracked run that someone confirms.

"Nothing: a proposed run only previews" is better because it reads the run's type and state together, and a proposed run never deploys, whatever the log says.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Yes, GO means a reviewer signed off”?
check:1:0.a:
"Yes, GO means a reviewer signed off" gets one thing right: GO is good news. On a proposed run, the GO after **Evaluated N plan policies** means the plan policies passed. Plan policies are rules the platform team wrote, such as "never destroy a PROD catalog." Spacelift checks the plan against them automatically.

What it misses is that no person is behind that GO. Every GO line marks one automatic step passing: the plan ran, its JSON was made, the resource list was uploaded, the policies passed. Someone may well have looked at the pull request too. But GO doesn't show that. Answering "yes" reports something the log never said.

It also blurs what a proposed run is. It only previews. Even with every GO, nothing was deployed. A person confirms a deploy later, on a tracked run waiting in `UNCONFIRMED`, because the stack has `autodeploy = false`.

"No, GO is an automatic check passing" is better because it states exactly what the log proves. Any human review is a separate question, and you check it in the pull request.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Yes, GO means it has been deployed”?
check:1:2.a:
That answer makes two mistakes at once.

First, it mixes up "checked" with "deployed." This was a **proposed** run, which is a preview. Spacelift plans it, reports to the pull request, and stops. A proposed run never deploys anything, whatever its log says. So if a pull request changes `grp-sales-dev-owners` permissions on a team folder, nothing has changed in the DEV workspace yet.

Second, it answers a different question. The manager asked whether *someone approved* it. The answer jumps to "deployed," which is a bigger claim and still wrong.

The answer does get one small thing right. GO does mean something passed. But every GO line in the planning log is an automatic step: the plan ran, its JSON (a machine-readable copy of the plan) was made, the resource list was uploaded. The GO after **Evaluated N plan policies** means the policy rules found no problem. No person was involved.

Deploying only happens on a **tracked** run, after someone confirms it.

"No, GO is an automatic check passing" is better because it answers the manager's actual question and says exactly what GO proves: a rule passed, not a person approving.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Tracked: it plans, then it applies”?
check:2:0.a:
"Tracked: it plans, then it applies" describes tracked runs correctly. A tracked run does plan first and then apply, which means it makes the real changes in Azure Databricks. The problem is that this push doesn't start a tracked run.

What decides the run type is the branch you pushed to. The stack's `branch` setting names its **tracked branch**, here `main`. Only pushes to `main` start tracked runs. Your push went to a feature branch, so Spacelift starts a **proposed** run instead.

Picture it on the `dbx-service-dev` stack. You push `feature/iac-review` with a new folder permission for `grp-sales-dev-owners`. Spacelift plans the change, posts the result to your pull request, and stops. Nothing touches the DEV workspace. The real change only happens later, when the code is merged into `main` and a tracked run is confirmed.

So the tempting answer mixes up "a run started" with "a deploy started." On a feature branch, it's always a preview.

"Proposed: it plans and reports back" is better because a push to any branch other than the tracked one only ever starts a preview, never a deploy.

check:2:1.q: Why not “None: a feature branch starts nothing”?
check:2:1.a:
"None" gets one thing right. A push to a feature branch never deploys anything. On a stack that tracks `main`, nothing reaches your Databricks workspace from that push.

But "nothing" goes too far. The question itself says a run starts. And Spacelift really does start one. For a push to any branch that isn't the stack's tracked branch, it starts a **proposed** run. That is a preview-only run.

Take the `dbx-service-dev` stack, which tracks `main`. A push to `feature/iac-review` starts a proposed run. It plans the change, for example adding `grp-sales-dev-owners` to a team's folder permissions. It runs the plan policies. It reports the result back to the pull request. Then it stops. Nothing is applied.

That preview is the whole point of a review. It is how you see what would change before anyone touches DEV, UAT or PROD.

"Proposed: it plans and reports back" is better because it describes what Spacelift actually does. It starts a real run that only previews and never deploys.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Upgrade providers on purpose” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
A **provider** is the plugin Terraform uses to talk to a platform. `azurerm` talks to Azure. Two files decide which version you get:

- The **constraint** in your code, like `~> 4.0`, means "any 4.x version is fine."
- The **lock file**, `.terraform.lock.hcl`, records the exact version last chosen, like `3.116.0`.

When they disagree, Terraform stops before planning. Your proposed run shows FAILED, and the first error in the planning log is that "does not match configured version constraint" line.

Here is how it bites in real work. Someone edits the constraint to `~> 4.0` for the `dbx-service-dev` stack. They don't update the lock file. Every pull request on that stack now fails to plan. The `team-sales` cluster change waiting for review is stuck too.

The quick fix is risky. A jump from 3.x to 4.x can rename settings or replace resources. That could touch `grp-sales-dev-owners` permissions.

So upgrade on purpose:

1. Run `terraform init -upgrade` in a branch.
2. Read the proposed run's Changes tab for surprise replacements.
3. Commit the new lock file with the change.

Then every run uses the version you actually reviewed.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. The phrase "The quick fix is risky" never says what the quick fix is, and the 3.x to 4.x claim goes slightly beyond the lesson, but neither contradicts it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that a run was misread:**

- Someone says "it's deployed" because the pull request shows *Finished*. Then `grp-sales-dev-owners` still can't open their folder in the DEV workspace. That run was proposed. It only previewed.
- A review note says "approved" and points at GO lines in the planning log. GO lines are automatic checks passing. None of them is a person saying yes.
- The **Changes** tab said "1 to add, 1 to destroy," but the review only mentioned the add. A replacement was missed. For example, a permission set for `team-sales` would be deleted and recreated.
- Changes appear in UAT that nobody expected. The reviewer never checked which environment or commit the header showed.
- A tracked run sits in UNCONFIRMED for days. Everyone thinks it already applied.

**Quickest check:** open the run and read the header first. Look at its type and state together. Then confirm the commit and the stack, such as `dbx-service-dev`. If you want proof of a deploy, look for a tracked run on `main` for that commit and check its state.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where reading a run's type and state needs extra care.

**1. The stack has `autodeploy = true`.** Then a tracked run skips `UNCONFIRMED` and applies right after planning, so `FINISHED` may mean no person ever looked. Check the stack's settings in the admin repo before you assume someone confirmed the `dbx-service-prod` apply.

**2. The preview goes stale.** A proposed run plans against the state as it was at that moment. If another team's change, say new grants for `grp-sales-dev-owners`, merges first, your old preview no longer matches. Read the tracked run's own plan before confirming it.

**3. Local preview is switched on.** With `enable_local_preview = true`, someone can start a preview from their laptop with code that was never pushed. The commit in the header may not match anything in `dbx-platform`. So trust only previews you can trace to a real commit on a pull request (a request to merge a branch).

judge.notes: Nothing contradicts the lesson. Points 2 and 3 go beyond it, and 'state' in point 2 is Terraform jargon left unexplained.

learn:term.a:
A **stack** is the long-lived setup. A **run** is one go of Terraform on that stack.

**Stack**: Spacelift's saved settings for one stage in one environment. It says which Git repository to read, which branch it tracks, and how deploys behave. It stays put and keeps its history.

**Run**: one event on that stack. It starts, plans, maybe applies, and ends in a state like `FINISHED` or `FAILED`. Every run belongs to exactly one stack.

Think of a weekly grocery delivery. The stack is your standing order: address, store, delivery rules. A run is one Tuesday's delivery. Many deliveries come from one order.

In the lesson, `dbx-service-dev` is the stack. It reads the `dbx-platform` repo and tracks `main`. Because of `autodeploy = false`, tracked runs wait for a person to confirm. Two pushes start two different kinds of run on it:

- A push to `main` starts a **tracked** run. It plans, then waits in `UNCONFIRMED` before applying.
- A pull request from `feature/iac-review` starts a **proposed** run. It plans, reports to the PR, and stops.

Same stack, different runs.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claim that a stack 'keeps its history' goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:0:0.a:
"Straight after network" gets one thing right. `jobs` does run because of the `network` change. It sits downstream: `network` → `workspace` → `catalogs` → `jobs`. And it can't go before `network` finishes.

What it misses is who `jobs` actually waits for. It doesn't wait for `network` directly. It waits for `workspace` and `catalogs`. Both of those are also running in this change, because they sit downstream of `network` too.

If `jobs` went straight after `network`, it could try to apply too early. Say `workspace` is still updating the Databricks workspace for team-sales. Or `catalogs` hasn't finished the catalog that sp-sales-etl-dev reads from. Then the `jobs` apply would point at things that aren't ready yet. The apply is the step where Terraform makes the real changes.

Think of the relay race. The `jobs` runner can't leave just because the first runner started. They need the baton from every runner handing it to them.

"Once workspace and catalogs have both finished" is better because it names exactly the stacks `jobs` waits for, and it only lets `jobs` start when every one of them is done.

check:0:2.q: Why not “At the same time as workspace”?
check:0:2.a:
"At the same time as `workspace`" gets one thing right. `jobs` does run after this `network` change. It is downstream: it waits for `workspace`, which waits for `network`. So Spacelift will start a run for it.

What it misses is the waiting. A stack only starts once every stack it waits for has finished. `jobs` waits for `workspace`, so it cannot run alongside it. Picture `jobs` creating a job for `team-sales` that runs as `sp-sales-etl-dev`. If the workspace is still being changed, that job has nothing stable to land in.

It also misses the second wait. `jobs` waits for `catalogs` too, and `catalogs` itself waits for `workspace`. So the real chain is `workspace`, then `catalogs`, then `jobs`. If `jobs` started early, its job might point at a catalog that doesn't exist yet.

Think of the relay race. A runner leaves only when every runner handing them the baton has arrived. `jobs` has two batons coming in, and one of them arrives last.

"Once `workspace` and `catalogs` have both finished" is better because it respects every stack `jobs` waits for, not just the one that changed first.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Yes, every stack runs on a change”?
check:1:0.a:
"Yes, every stack runs on a change" gets one thing right. A change in `network` does trigger more than one run. Spacelift also starts runs for the stacks that depend on `network`, like `workspace`. So the change does spread.

What it misses is *where* the change spreads. It only moves **downstream**. That means it follows the "waits for" links, from a stack to the stacks that wait for it, then to the stacks that wait for those. A stack runs only if there is a chain of those links back to the change.

`billing` waits for nothing. No link connects it to `network`, directly or through another stack. So nothing about the `network` change reaches it, and it does not run.

That is on purpose. Imagine a small subnet tweak in DEV kicking off plans for every stack on the platform. You would get slow runs, extra approvals and more chances for surprises. Skipping unrelated stacks keeps a small change small.

"No, it doesn't depend on network" is better because it names the real rule: only stacks connected to the change by dependencies run.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Yes, but only after workspace”?
check:1:2.a:
"Yes, but only after workspace" gets one thing right. Order does matter in Spacelift. A stack that runs has to wait until every stack it waits for has finished.

But that rule only sorts stacks that are already running. It never adds new ones. First Spacelift decides **who runs**, then it decides **in what order**.

So start with who runs. When `network` changes, Spacelift follows the "waits for" links outward from `network`. Those links lead to `workspace`, and then to anything that waits for `workspace`. That is the **downstream** set: every stack linked back to the change, directly or through another stack.

`billing` waits for nothing. No link connects it to `network`, so it is not downstream. It does not run at all, so the question of when it runs never comes up.

The answer also adds a wait that isn't there. `billing` does not wait for `workspace`, so "after workspace" has no basis.

This is what keeps a small change small. A subnet tweak in `network` shouldn't trigger a `billing` run in DEV, UAT or PROD.

"No, it doesn't depend on network" is better because it checks who runs first, and `billing` has no link to `network` at all.

judge.notes: Minor wording issue: 'follows the waits-for links outward from network' blurs the direction, since the links point from workspace to network. Otherwise it matches the lesson and is just under 200 words.

check:2:0.a:
That answer gets two things right. `workspace` runs because it changed. `catalogs` runs because it waits for `workspace`, so it sits **downstream** (further along the chain of stacks that depend on something).

The mistake is including `network`. Runs only flow downstream, away from the change. They never flow back **upstream** (toward the stacks a changed stack depends on).

`network` is upstream of `workspace`. `workspace` needs the subnets `network` already made. But a change in `workspace` doesn't touch those subnets. Nothing in `network`'s code or state is different, so Spacelift has no reason to run it.

What about the rule that `workspace` waits for `network`? That wait only matters if `network` is running too. Here it isn't, so `workspace` can start right away.

Think of a team-sales update to a workspace setting. It shouldn't re-plan the platform team's network in DEV, UAT or PROD. Leaving `network` alone keeps a small change small.

"`workspace`, then `catalogs`" is better because it runs only the changed stack and what depends on it, in waiting order.

check:2:1.a:
"Only workspace" gets half of it right. `workspace` changed, so it runs. And `network` does not run, because `network` sits *upstream* (before `workspace` in the chain). A change never flows backwards.

What it misses is the *downstream* part. Downstream means every stack that waits for the changed one, directly or through another stack. `catalogs` waits for `workspace`. So when `workspace` applies a change, Spacelift starts a run for `catalogs` too.

Think about what `catalogs` does. It might create the Unity Catalog catalogs for `team-sales` and grant `grp-sales-dev-owners` access, all inside that workspace. If the workspace changed, those catalogs need a fresh plan to check they still match. Skipping `catalogs` could leave it out of step with the workspace it lives in.

Order matters as well. `catalogs` only starts once `workspace` has finished. That is the relay-race rule: a runner leaves only when the runner handing them the baton has arrived.

"workspace, then catalogs" is better because it includes the stack downstream of the change and runs it after the stack it waits for.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A stack runs too early.** The `jobs` plan fails with "catalog not found" because `catalogs` hasn't applied yet. You rerun it and it passes. A run that fails and then passes with no code change often means the order was wrong. (A *plan* is Terraform's preview of changes. An *apply* makes them.)
- **A stack never runs.** `network` changed, but `catalogs` kept old settings. Everything looks green. Later, PROD doesn't match the code. That mismatch is called *drift*.
- **Too many stacks run.** A change to `catalogs` also starts `monitoring`, which doesn't wait for it. The run queue fills up, and a small change no longer stays small.
- **The order shifts between runs.** Two stacks are both ready, but they swap places from one run to the next. Results become hard to repeat, because nothing settles which ready stack goes first.

**Quickest check**

Pick one real change, such as `network` in DEV. Using the dependency list, write down by hand who should run and in what order. Then open Spacelift's run history, the list of past runs with their start and finish times. Compare the two. Every stack should start only after all the stacks it waits for have finished. No extra stacks should appear.

judge.notes: No real problems; the answer is about 205 words, which is borderline on length but acceptable.

learn:stops.a:
The rule works well for a small, healthy set of stacks. Here are three places it needs extra care.

**A loop of waits.** Say `catalogs` waits for `jobs` and `jobs` also waits for `catalogs`. Neither can ever start, so the ordering step gets stuck with stacks left over and none ready. Check for loops (a "cycle") first, and fix the dependency in the admin repo.

**An upstream run fails.** The rule assumes every run finishes cleanly. If `workspace` fails its policy check in UAT, then `catalogs` and `jobs` should not run on a half-built workspace. Skip everything downstream of a failed stack, and rerun it after the fix.

**Many stacks.** With dozens of stacks per environment, one at a time in name order gets slow. Stacks whose waits are all done can safely run side by side, in parallel, like `monitoring` and `workspace` in the example. Spacelift can do this for you.

judge.notes: No real problems. The only loose point is 'Spacelift can do this for you', which the lesson does not state, but it does not contradict the lesson either.

learn:term.a:
**Spacelift** is the tool. A **stack** is one piece of work that the tool runs.

Spacelift is a service that runs Terraform for you. It watches your code. When the code changes, it makes a plan (a preview of what will change), runs policy checks, and applies the change once approved. It also remembers which stacks wait for which.

A stack is one Terraform folder with its own state. "State" is Terraform's record of what it has already built. In this lesson, `network`, `workspace`, `monitoring`, `catalogs` and `jobs` are each a separate stack.

Think of an airport. Spacelift is the control tower. Each stack is one plane. The tower decides when each plane leaves. It knows which planes must arrive before another can go.

Here is how they work together. When `network` changes, Spacelift notices. It starts runs for every stack downstream, meaning every stack that waits for `network`, directly or through another stack. Then it puts them in order: `monitoring`, `workspace`, `catalogs`, `jobs`. `jobs` goes last because it waits for both `workspace` and `catalogs`.

So there is one Spacelift and many stacks.
